transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
The media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico square off against the Trump administration
in federal court this morning.
It's over access to the White House.
The White House has sought to ban their reporters, citing national security concerns.
But President Trump announced he was doing so because he didn't like their coverage.
As NPR's David Falkenflick reports, the news outlets say he's violating their First Amendment
rights.
A federal judge forced the White House to pause its ban.
Now he'll consider what to do about it.
Legal presidents suggest Trump didn't have to let them in.
But once he did, he can't keep them out simply because of their coverage.
CNN is still being periodically blocked from taking part in a TV pool in which the network
shares costs and logistics of covering the president's actions in public spaces with
four other networks that footage is shared widely.
The White House has blocked CNN from operating in smaller places for the pool, like Air Force
One.
The judge has to assess that, too.
David Falkenflick, NPR News.
The third quarter of 2026 represented the most dangerous period for global shipping
in recent history.
That's according to maritime intelligence group Windward.
For the first time, four major navies belonging to Iran, Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. struck
merchant ships, turning commercial vessels into tools of interstate conflict.
And Piers Hadil Al-Shelchi reports.
The maritime intelligence firm Windward said that the overall traffic in the Strait of
Hormuz has doubled since July, but that the actual number of tankers passing through this
waterway may be higher, driven by the U.S. Navy escorting night convoys traveling in Omani
waters.
The tanker traffic in the Red Sea waterway of Bab al-Mandeb dropped by 26 percent due
to Iranian-backed Houthi attacks on Saudi vessels, according to the group.
It said Iran shifted its strategy between July and September, changing from indiscriminate
attacks to specifically target tankers navigating the U.S.-protected southern corridor.
Nearly half of the targeted vessels belong to the national fleets of Gulf energy companies.
Hadil Al-Shelchi, NPR News.
Russia bombed a public bus in an eastern Ukrainian fortress city, killing at least 30 people and
injuring another 18.
Piers Juana Kakissis reports from Kyiv.
Russia used guided aerial bombs to strike the bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk.
This city and the neighboring town of Slovyansk are the last two major settlements in the
Donetsk region under Ukrainian control.
Writing on social media, the region's governor, Vadim Filoshkin, said, "Russia comes to Ukrainian
land with death."
Filoshkin said public transportation in Kramatorsk and Slovyansk has been halted for safety reasons.
Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian cities ahead of winter, striking homes as
well as power and water facilities.
Joanna Kakissis, NPR News, Kyiv.
This is NPR.
Hurricane Isaias is swirling nearly 400 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River.
Top winds are at 80 miles per hour.
The storm could make landfall on the Gulf Coast tomorrow night.
Forecasters say it will be strong.
More than 4,000 plaintiffs across the country are suing drug makers, claiming serious harms
from GLP-1 drugs.
NPR's Yuki Noguchi reports this raises questions about how common such side effects may be.
Millions of Americans take these drugs, yet there isn't much reliable data about serious
side effects, like sudden blindness, pancreatitis, and gallstones.
Osempics maker Novo Nordisk says serious conditions are exceedingly rare in clinical trials.
The Food and Drug Administration tracks side effect reports filed by doctors, patients
or companies.
NPR found about 2,000 cases of pancreatitis and 1,000 cases of sudden blindness out of
190,000 GLP-1-related findings since 2024.
But those reports are unverified, and doctors often don't report because it's hard to
be sure the drugs caused the problems.
Yuki Noguchi, NPR News.
The winner of this year's Nobel Prize in Literature is Canadian author Anne Carson.
She is a poet, essayist and professor of classics.
The Nobel Committee pointed to her use of ancient Greek and Roman themes for her works.
Tomorrow, the renowned Nobel Peace Prize will be awarded; the Economics Prize will be presented
on Monday.
You're listening to NPR.

Federal judge pauses White House ban on news outlets, considers legality of restricting reporter access
Q3 2026 marked most dangerous period for global shipping as four major navies targeted merchant vessels
Iranian-backed Houthis attack Saudi vessels in Red Sea, reducing tanker traffic through Bab al-Mandeb by 26 percent
Russia bombs public bus in Kramatorsk, eastern Ukrainian city, killing at least 30 people and injuring 18
Hurricane Isaias swirling 400 miles south of Mississippi River mouth with 80 mph winds, landfall possible tomorrow night
